Assume the beam is straight, prismatic, and has a rectangular cross-section of width b and height h.
Assume the material is homogeneous, isotropic, and linear elastic with Young's modulus E.
Assume Euler-Bernoulli beam theory: plane sections remain plane and perpendicular to the deformed neutral axis, and transverse shear deformation is neglected.
Assume small deformations so the curvature is approximated by the second derivative of the transverse deflection.
Let the beam axis be x, let y be measured from the centroidal neutral axis, and let the bending moment act about the z-axis.
Let the internal bending moment at a section be M_z(x), determined from equilibrium of the applied loads and moments.
The neutral axis is located at the centroid of the rectangular cross-section, so it is at y = 0.
The area moment of inertia about the z-axis is I_z = b h^3 / 12.
The bending normal stress at an arbitrary fiber location y is sigma_x(x,y) = - M_z(x) y / I_z.
The bending strain at an arbitrary fiber is epsilon_x(x,y) = sigma_x(x,y) / E = - M_z(x) y / (E I_z).
The maximum bending stress magnitude occurs at the outer fibers y = +h/2 and y = -h/2 and is |sigma_max| = 6 |M_z(x)| / (b h^2).
The curvature of the beam neutral axis is kappa(x) = M_z(x) / (E I_z).
The transverse deflection w(x) satisfies d^2 w/dx^2 = M_z(x) / (E I_z).
If transverse shear forces are present, the bending normal stress formula remains valid away from concentrated load application points and supports, while shear stresses are distributed parabolically over the cross-section.
If an additional axial force N(x) is present, add the uniform axial stress N(x) / (b h) to the bending stress using superposition.
If the applied moment has components about more than one axis, resolve it into components and superimpose the bending stresses using the corresponding area moments of inertia.
